title: MCP: a standard for connecting tools

opening.headline: We examine how the common specification MCP reduces the problem of having to write new code every time an agent is connected to an external system.
body: When connecting agents to internal databases, document repositories, and ticketing systems, you end up repeatedly creating similar connection codes for each agent. If each system uses different authentication methods and response formats, every change to one system requires updates in multiple locations.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open-source standard that unifies the way AI applications connect to external systems. In this course, we will sequentially examine the components of MCP, the three primitives provided by the server—transport mechanisms, and connection methods from three different companies. Finally, we will distinguish between the problems that MCP solves and those that remain unresolved for designers.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the composition (host, client, server) of MCP and the primitives (tools, resources, prompts) exposed by the server.
It is possible to distinguish the problems that MCP resolves from those it does not resolve and leaves unresolved.

screens.title: Create a new connection code for each tool
screens.lead: Read about how the number of connections changes as agents and systems increase. The following diagram compares the same scenario in two different ways.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing side by side the individual connections of 12 links between 3 agents and 4 systems, and the reduced number of 7 links after passing through a common standard.

paragraphs: The company has three types of agents, and there are four systems that need to be connected: internal database, document repository, ticketing system, and messaging service. If a unique connection code is created for each agent-system pair, there would be 3 × 4, or 12 connections.

If each connection uses a different authentication method and response format, the problem becomes significantly worse. If the API of one system changes, the code of all agents attached to that system must be updated. Even if you add a new agent, you'll need to reestablish the connection with all four systems from scratch.

If a common standard is established for connecting AI applications with external tools and data, the number of connections reduces from seven—three on the agent side and four on the server side. This standard is known as MCP. The MCP document draws an analogy to a USB-C port for AI applications, meaning that instead of using different cables for each device, a single standard specification is used to connect them.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When connections are unified into one, redundancy in connection codes is reduced. But will problems such as poorly named or poorly documented tools, or inadequate permission design also disappear? We answer this question at the end of the lesson.

screens.outro: First, let us recall your experience connecting the system to the agent.

screens.title: Preview: Internal system connection experience
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: When connecting the internal system to an agent, who and where organized the authentication information and invocation format?
items.answer: Typically, this information remains only in the code or notes of the person who first established the connection. Since the methods vary from system to system, someone else must discover them from scratch when performing the same task. A common standard collects this information into a predefined location known as the server's tool definition.

items.prompt: When you attached the same system to a second agent, how many times did you have to rewrite the code?
items.answer: If agents use different frameworks or invocation methods, they are effectively forced to be rewritten. MCP targets reuse by establishing a single server that multiple hosts can connect to using the same method.

items.prompt: Was there a device where a person would verify when an agent attempted a write operation?
items.answer: This question cannot be answered solely based on the connection specification. The specification recommends that tools include mechanisms that humans can reject, but the designator must determine exactly what actions require confirmation. This is addressed again in the final screen.

screens.outro: We will compare the recalled experience with the structure of the following screen.

screens.title: MCP Architecture: Host, Client, Server
screens.lead: When you select the number marker of the diagram, you can view the detailed role of the corresponding component. Please select them in order from number 1.

visual.alt: Three clients inside the host are each connected one-to-one to a respective server, forming a structure where the server exposes tools, resources, and prompts.
labels: The entire conversation is not visible on the server.

markers.label: host
markers.title: Host: Container and orchestrator
markers.body: The host is the AI application itself. It creates and manages multiple client instances, controls client connection permissions and lifecycles. It enforces security policies and user consent requirements, and aggregates context from multiple clients.

markers.label: client
markers.title: Client: Server with exact 1:1
markers.body: The client communicates with only one server that the host creates. The host may have multiple clients, but clients and servers always maintain a 1:1 relationship. The client attaches the protocol version and capabilities to all requests, bidirectionally transmits protocol messages, and maintains the security boundary between servers.

markers.label: server
markers.title: Server: Expose tools, resources, and prompts
markers.body: The server provides specific contexts and functionalities. It exposes primitives such as tools, resources, and prompts, which may be local processes or remote services. Each server focuses on a narrow and well-defined role and operates independently.

markers.label: Design Principles
markers.title: The server is easy to build and easy to combine, but it cannot see the conversation.
markers.body: The design principles specified are that servers must be easy to build and easy to compose. The third principle is that servers must not be able to read the entire conversation or peek into other servers. Servers receive only the necessary context, and the full conversation history remains under the host's control. Server-to-server interactions are also governed and controlled by the host.

markers.label: message
markers.title: Self-contained complete request as described in JSON-RPC above
markers.body: The message arrives via JSON-RPC. In the revised specification, MCP is a stateless protocol where all requests are self-contained and include their own protocol version and capabilities. The server can announce its capabilities in the response, enabling progressive extension by negotiating only the required features.

screens.outro: I will continue to verify who controls the three primitives exposed by the server.

screens.title: Tools, resources, prompts: Who controls them?
screens.lead: The following flashcard describes three primitives exposed by the MCP server. Select the card to flip it. Use the right arrow to advance to the next card.

visual.alt: Three icons representing tools, resources, and prompts.

cards.back: This is an execution function that the model invokes autonomously by observing the context of a conversation. Examples include database queries, API calls, and computations. Each tool has a unique name and schema metadata. For security, users must be able to reject calls, and the specification recommends providing a UI that displays available tools and prompts for confirmation upon invocation.

This data specifies how the host application inserts context. File content or database schema are typical examples, identified by URI. Unlike tools, the model does not retrieve this context on its own; instead, the application selects and inserts it.

This is a template explicitly chosen by the user. It is exposed like a slash command and constructs a pre-defined message by accepting parameters. It allows the user to load a workflow for repetitive tasks at once.

The server declares the primitives it supports as capabilities. For example, only a server that declares tools will respond to a tools/list request. This declaration enables clients and servers to use only the functionalities they need and to gradually expand their capabilities over time.

screens.outro: Let's examine how the tool appears in the actual message by looking at the code.

screens.title: Server capability declaration and reading the tools/list response
screens.lead: The following describes the server declaring that it has tools and responding to the client's tools/list request. Check the symptoms when there is a mismatch between the meaning and value of each line in the right-hand description.

notes.note: This section declares the server's tools capability. Only servers that declare tools must respond to a tools/list request. If listChanged is true, it means the server will send notifications when the tool list changes. Exposing tools without declaring them may cause the client to not request tools, resulting in an empty tool list.

name is the unique identifier of the tool, and description is the basis on which the model selects the tool. If names overlap or descriptions are ambiguous, the model may incorrectly select a tool. Since the model reads only this text, distinct names and clear descriptions—written as if explaining to a new team member—are most important in these two lines.

The inputSchema defines the shape of the call arguments. The property customer_id is defined as a string and included in the required field to indicate it is mandatory. Arguments not listed in required may be omitted; therefore, if a required value is omitted, the model will omit the argument during the call and throw an error.

result.tools is a list of currently available tools. It may be empty and can change over time. The server should consistently rotate through the list in the same order, so that clients can cache the list and achieve higher prompt cache hit rates.

screens.outro: We will examine which pathway the server is connected through and how the three companies set this up.

screens.title: Transmission method and MCP connections with three companies
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare MCP's transmission methods and connection approaches to OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google Cloud.

tabs.label: Transmission method
tabs.body:
**stdio** communicates with local processes on the same device via standard input and output. For **remote HTTP** (Streamable HTTP), the server receives POST requests from clients and responds with JSON or SSE streams through a single MCP endpoint.

The remote server must validate the Origin header and provide authentication. The specification recommends that servers launched locally bind only to 127.0.0.1, not to all network interfaces.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body:
The Responses API defines a `tools` entry of type `mcp` and specifies `server_label` and `server_url`. It also determines whether approval is required for each call via the `require_approval` field.

```json
{"type": "mcp", "server_label": "orders", "server_url": "https://orders.example.com/mcp", "require_approval": "always"}
```

Before setting it to `never`, double-check whether this is a read-only public server. Private servers not exposed externally can be connected without exposure via Secure MCP Tunnel.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body:
Place servers in the `mcp_servers` of the Messages API, and place the `mcp_toolset` in the `tools`. You can either allow all tools or restrict them with an allowlist or blocklist.

```json
"mcp_servers": [{"type": "url", "url": "https://example-server.modelcontextprotocol.io/sse", "name": "example-mcp", "authorization_token": "<OAuth token>"}],
"tools": [{"type": "mcp_toolset", "mcp_server_name": "example-mcp"}]
```

The `url` must begin with `https://`, and the `name` must match the `mcp_server_name`. The `authorization_token` is used when the server requires OAuth. This connector supports only tool invocation functionality within the MCP framework, and the server must be publicly accessible via HTTP. A custom connector for Claude users connects to remote MCP servers, and since the connection originates from the Anthropic cloud, private network servers require firewall access.

tabs.label: Google Cloud
tabs.body:
Google Cloud enables agents to use Google and Google Cloud services through a remote MCP server, while providing governance, security, and access control features. A standalone MCP server can be published using Apigee or Cloud Run.

All three companies provide their own control mechanisms—such as approval lists, permitting lists, and access controls—on the same standard framework. While the standard is the same, the control configurations have different names and locations depending on the product.

screens.outro: Having examined the structure and configuration, we will now illustrate an example of exposing a corporate database to an MCP server.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Exposing Internal Database to MCP Server
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of connecting the order database to the agent, as well as issues encountered by team members with their initial setup. Select the right arrow to proceed step by step.

visual.alt: Path from cloud-side host to the MCP server and order database within the internal network via the Internet.

steps.title: Step 1: The server determines what it will offer
steps.body: We do not directly expose the order database. Instead, the server provides a few tools with clear purposes, such as `search_orders`, along with resources that describe the schema. The database account used by the server is set to read-only. The principle of minimizing tool count and clearly naming tools and descriptions is also applied here.

steps.title: Step 2: The initial settings entered by the team member
steps.body:
A team member configured the host as follows:

```json
"mcp_servers": [{"type": "url", "url": "http://orders.internal/mcp", "name": "orders"}],
"tools": [{"type": "mcp_toolset", "mcp_server_name": "order-db"}]
```

When attempting to connect, the tool list is empty or the connection is rejected. Investigate directly to determine the issue.

steps.title: Step 3: Read Configuration
steps.body: First, `url` starts with `http://`. This field must start with `https://`. Second, `mcp_server_name` is `order-db`, but the server's `name` is `orders`. If the names do not match, the tool set will not be able to locate the server. The symptom is either an empty tool list or a connection rejection.

steps.title: Step 4: Modify Settings
steps.body: Replace `url` with `https://` and replace `mcp_server_name` with `orders`. If the server requires OAuth, also include `authorization_token`. After making the changes, verify that the server declares tools capability and responds with `tools/list`.

steps.title: Step 5: Verify Reachability Path
steps.body: If the host is in the cloud and the server is within the corporate network, the connection originates from the cloud, so the server must be accessible via a public path. If it is not accessible, firewall rules must be configured or a tunnel established. Origin verification and authentication must be applied to the remote server. The key point is that simply because a server is publicly accessible does not mean data is exposed—never leave servers open without authentication.

steps.title: Step 6: Call and Authorization
steps.body: When the model selects a tool, the host receives confirmation, and the server returns the result. Since the server cannot see the entire conversation, it only receives the necessary parameters. Order lookup is read-only and can be automatically permitted; however, if a write tool for modifying an order is added, it should be placed behind the approval stage.

screens.outro: The connection is complete, so let's move on to a summary distinguishing what the MCP resolves and what it leaves unresolved.

screens.title: What MCP resolves versus what it leaves behind
screens.lead: Select an item to expand and distinguish between issues resolved by the specification and those remaining for the designer. Each item can be opened and closed independently.

items.title: Resolving: Unification of connection specifications
items.body: A single server can be reused by multiple hosts. Since the tool list, schema, and call format are all identical, the 3 × 4 connection previously described reduces to 3 + 4. If one system changes, only the server needs to be updated.

items.title: Issue 1: Tool quality
items.body: Even if specifications are the same, if the name, description, or response quality is poor, the model incorrectly identifies the tool. As more servers are added, the number of tools increases accordingly, and the problem of reduced selection accuracy becomes evident when the number of tools exceeds 30 to 50. MCP only specifies how to connect tools; it does not create high-quality tools.

items.title: Issue 2: Authorization and Security
items.body: Authorization is based on OAuth and is optional rather than mandatory. Security best practices documentation outlines risks such as the confused deputy attack, where an authorization code is obtained by a proxy server without user consent. Authorization and access control must be handled directly by the designer.

items.title: Issue 3: Reachability, Approval, Version
items.body: Methods for reaching the external network server, distinction between read and write operations, and points where a human can verify are determined by the designer. Specifications are differentiated by revision date and transmission methods have evolved; therefore, the host and server must align on the revisions they support.

items.title: How to Read Errors: Two Signals
items.body:
Unknown tools, malformed requests, or server errors are treated as JSON-RPC errors. Issues with the request structure are difficult for models to correct on their own, and the host or server developer must identify and resolve the root cause.

In contrast, if the response contains entries such as `"isError": true` or "Invalid departure date: must be in the future," these indicate input validation or business rule errors. Presenting these messages directly to the model allows it to correct the date and reissue the request. The entity responsible for correction depends on the specific signal.

screens.outro: Since the distinction is complete, I will now summarize the entire MCP on a single page.

screens.title: Summarize MCP into one page
screens.lead: This summarizes the structure, primitives, transmission, and remaining issues in a single flow.

paragraphs: The host creates a client, and one client connects to one server. The server exposes tools, resources, and prompts. Tools are managed by the model, resources by the application, and prompts are controlled by the user.

Transmission is either local stdio or remote HTTP, with authentication and Origin verification applied for remote access. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google Cloud each provide their own controls, such as approval and allowance lists, under the same standard.

Let's go back to the first question. Once connections are unified, redundant connection codes are reduced. However, design issues such as tool names and descriptions, permissions, and approval points do not disappear. Standards unify connections but do not replace design.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: MCP is a specification for tool connectivity. It reduces redundancy in connections, but creating good tools and designing safe permissions remains the designer's responsibility.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Pair the three exposures of the MCP server with the entities that control them.
right: A template explicitly chosen and used by the user
A model's execution function that calls itself autonomously based on observing the situation
Data that defines how the host application places context
checks.explain: The tool is called by the model, resources are included in the application's context, and the prompt is set by the user like a slash command.

checks.intro: Issue reading error response. Result is not recorded.
checks.q:
The MCP tool call result is as follows. What correctly interprets this situation?  
{"result": {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Invalid departure date: must be in the future"}], "isError": true}}
options: This is a protocol error that has broken the request structure, so it is hidden from the model and fixed by the developer.
The server is down, so we need to switch to another transmission method.
Due to input validation error, directly pass it to the model to let it correct it and re-call itself.
Since the tool succeeded, it is displayed to the user as is, regardless of isError.
checks.explain: Results where isError is true indicate execution errors such as input validation failures or business rule violations. These can be shown to the model, allowing it to correct the date and retry the call. Unknown tools or broken requests are handled separately as JSON-RPC errors.

wrong.0: A malformed request arrives as a JSON-RPC error here, and in this case, it came via isError in the result.
wrong.1: The server responded normally; the only issue was with the input values.
wrong.3: If isError is true, then the call has failed. It should not be treated as a successful result.

glossary.def: As an AI application, it handles creating clients and managing connection permissions, security policies, and user consent.
This exposes tools, resources, and prompts. It could be a local process or a remote service.
The basic components exposed by the server are tools, resources, and prompts.
This is a remote transmission method where the server responds to a POST request with JSON or SSE stream through a single MCP endpoint.
An attack in which a proxy server tricks a user into granting an authorization code without their consent, listed as a risk in the MCP security documentation.
This indicates an execution error in the tool call result. If true, it allows displaying the body to the model to prompt it for a retry.

misconceptions.myth: Using MCP eliminates the need to worry about tool design.
misconceptions.fact: The specification is only about the connection method. If the name, description, or response is poor, the selection error remains unchanged.

misconceptions.myth: The MCP server can see the entire conversation.
misconceptions.fact: By design, the server receives only the necessary context. The entire conversation history is retained by the host, and the server cannot peek into other servers.

misconceptions.myth: The MCP server sticks right onto anywhere.
misconceptions.fact: In the approach of connecting from the cloud, the server must be reachable via a public path. Servers within a private network require firewall allowances or tunnels.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: MCP is the specification for tool connectivity. It is divided into host, client, and server, with a 1:1 relationship between client and server.
The server exposes tools (model invocations), resources (application context inclusion), and prompts (user-selected).
Transmission is via stdio or remote HTTP, and each of the three companies provides its own approval and allowance lists under the same specifications.
The specification resolves redundancy in connections; tool design quality, authorization, and approval of design remain outstanding.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Where in my tool connections are there duplicate codes, and which ones can be consolidated into a single server?
